new_statements.quote: Stress always seems to occur on the first heavy syllable of the word. Words with syllables of equal weight usually have stress on the first syllable.
new_statements.citation: Stutzman, Robert & Verna Stutzman. 1992. Tauade Organised Phonology Data. Manuscript (draft), 4 pp. Ukarumpa: SIL Papua New Guinea. SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 42361, https://www.sil.org/resources/archives/42361
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (PDF 1.4, 4 pp, text layer, pdfinfo title 'OPD', author 'SIL PNG Branch', printed 2004-09-07). extracted text shows, on physical page 3 (footer 'Tauade OPD Printed: September 7, 2004 Page 3'), the heading 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' followed by exactly: 'Stress always seems to occur on the first heavy syllable of the word. Words with syllables of equal weight usually have stress on the first syllable.' Quote matches the report verbatim (single line-break at 'weight / usually' in the PDF). Immediately below is the 'Syllable Patterns' table listing V, VC, VV, CV, CVC, CVV, CVVC with examples (ip 'water', au 'but', val 'back', mii 'shoot', kaut 'lime', pu.lait 'bean'), so '…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the leftmost heavy syllable of the word; if all syllables are of equal weight (no heavy syllable, or all equally heavy), stress defaults to the initial syllable. The OPD's syllable-pattern table (p. 3) lists VC, VV, CVC, CVV, CVVC alongside V and CV, so 'heavy' presumably means closed or long-vowel/diphthong syllables; the OPD does not define weight explicitly.
new_statements.exceptions: None listed; the statement is hedged ('always seems to', 'usually').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('of the word'); a 4-page SIL Organised Phonology Data sheet (draft, no peer review), based on the Stutzmans' fieldwork (data checked March 1992). No tone or length contrast is claimed in the suprasegmental section, though vowel sequences/long vowels (ii, ee, aa, oo, uu) appear in the inventory.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD describes Tauade [ttd] of Central Province (major village Sopu), labelled 'Goilalan Family' in the SIL sheet; Glottolog 5.1 treats taua1242 as an isolate. No dialect is specified. Alternate names in the record: Tauata, Afoa, Goilala, Ambo(-Deba).

sources.quote: Stress always seems to occur on the first heavy syllable of the word. Words with syllables of equal weight usually have stress on the first syllable.
sources.note: p. 3, 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': stress always seems to fall on the first heavy syllable of the word; words whose syllables are of equal weight usually stress the first syllable. Syllable-pattern table on the same page (V, VC, VV, CV, CVC, CVV, CVVC) shows closed and long-vowel/diphthong syllables, i.e. the heavy types.

No descriptive (grammar/phonology/sketch) references listed; only overviews (Dutton 1975, Ray 1929, Ray 1913-14) and wordlists (Egidi 1907, Strong 1912, Anonymous 1914, Humphries 1922, Fastre 1920). Nothing on stress.
Stub; no phonology section; notes PARADISEC TD1 (Dutton) holds Tauade materials.
